\chapter{Words That Join an Answer}
\label{ch:te-joining-words}
\hlchaptermodality{64}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can add to a Telugu answer, limit it, put it in order, or say it is not finished.}

Complete TE-C64-still and demonstrate the chapter promise.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kūḍā]{\te{కూడా} (kūḍā) — also}

\label{lesson:TE-C64-also}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{ārōgyaṁ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{కూడా}}
\textbf{\te{కూడా}} (\emph{kūḍā}) — \textquotedblleft{}also\textquotedblright{}.

\te{కూడా} goes after the thing it is adding, not before it. \te{నేను} \te{కూడా} is \textquotedblleft{}me too\textquotedblright{}; \te{పెరుగు} \te{కూడా} is \textquotedblleft{}the curd as well\textquotedblright{}.

English can drop \textquotedblleft{}also\textquotedblright{} almost anywhere in a sentence and let the stress carry the meaning. Telugu puts \te{కూడా} straight after whatever it includes, and that placement does the work the stress would have done.

It is a small word that softens a great deal. Adding \te{కూడా} to an answer turns a flat \te{అవును} into agreement with the person who asked.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first joining word.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kūḍā}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{nēnu kūḍā}, then \emph{perugu kūḍā}, and say what each one adds
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{కూడా} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}also\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mātramē]{\te{మాత్రమే} (mātramē) — only}

\label{lesson:TE-C64-only}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kūḍā} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{మాత్రమే}}
\textbf{\te{మాత్రమే}} (\emph{mātramē}) — \textquotedblleft{}only\textquotedblright{}.

\te{మాత్రమే} is the other half of \te{కూడా}. Where \te{కూడా} opens an answer out, \te{మాత్రమే} shuts it: \te{పెరుగు} \te{మాత్రమే} is \textquotedblleft{}curd and nothing else\textquotedblright{}. It stands in the same place, straight after the thing it is about.

It is built on Sanskrit \emph{mātra}, \textquotedblleft{}a measure\textquotedblright{} — the same piece English carries in metre and in diameter. Saying \te{మాత్రమే} is saying \textquotedblleft{}this much and no further\textquotedblright{}.

With a small quantity in front it does polite work. \te{కొంచెం} \te{మాత్రమే}, \textquotedblleft{}only a little\textquotedblright{}, accepts what is offered without taking much of it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two, and they pull opposite ways.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mātramē}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{perugu kūḍā}, then \emph{perugu mātramē}, and say which one takes more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{మాత్రమే} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}only\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ayitē]{\te{అయితే} (ayitē) — in that case}

\label{lesson:TE-C64-in-that-case}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{mātramē} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{అయితే}}
\textbf{\te{అయితే}} (\emph{ayitē}) — \textquotedblleft{}in that case\textquotedblright{}.

\te{అయితే} picks up what the other person has just said and turns on it: \te{సరే}, \te{అయితే} \te{వెళ్ళొస్తాను} — \textquotedblleft{}alright, in that case I'll be off\textquotedblright{}.

It is put together out of the piece Telugu uses for \textquotedblleft{}it happened\textquotedblright{} plus the little ending that means \textquotedblleft{}if\textquotedblright{}, so what it literally says is \textquotedblleft{}if it is so\textquotedblright{}. English \textquotedblleft{}well then\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}in that case\textquotedblright{} both land in the same spot.

At the head of an answer, on its own, \te{అయితే} is one of the most useful things a learner can carry. It buys a moment, and it shows the other person you were listening.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ayitē}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{sarē}, then \emph{ayitē}, and put the two together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{అయితే} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}in that case\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[taruvāta]{\te{తరువాత} (taruvāta) — after that, later}

\label{lesson:TE-C64-after}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{ayitē} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{తరువాత}}
\textbf{\te{తరువాత}} (\emph{taruvāta}) — \textquotedblleft{}after that, later\textquotedblright{}.

\te{తరువాత} puts two things in order: \emph{bhōjanaṁ taruvāta}, \textquotedblleft{}after the meal\textquotedblright{}. It goes after the thing it follows, exactly like \te{కూడా} and \te{మాత్రమే} before it — a habit worth noticing, because it holds for a great many of these small words.

The word is inherited. Standing alone at the front of a sentence it means \textquotedblleft{}later\textquotedblright{}, and it is the gentle way to put something off: \te{తరువాత}, not now, and no reason offered.

\te{తరువాత} is also how a story gets kept moving. A listener who says it is asking you to go on.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and this one is about order.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{taruvāta}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{bhōjanaṁ taruvāta}, then just \emph{taruvāta}, and say how the two differ
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{తరువాత} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}after that, later\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[iṅkā]{\te{ఇంకా} (iṅkā) — still, yet}

\label{lesson:TE-C64-still}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{taruvāta} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{ఇంకా}}
\textbf{\te{ఇంకా}} (\emph{iṅkā}) — \textquotedblleft{}still, yet\textquotedblright{}.

\te{ఇంకా} says the thing is not finished. \te{ఇంకా} \te{ఉంది} is \textquotedblleft{}there is still some\textquotedblright{}; \te{ఇంకా} \te{రాలేదు} is \textquotedblleft{}she hasn't come yet\textquotedblright{}.

It is the natural answer to \te{అంతే}. Where \te{అంతే} closes a list off, \te{ఇంకా} says there is more of it coming, and the two make a pair the way \te{కూడా} and \te{మాత్రమే} do.

Five small words, and not one of them names a thing. \te{కూడా}, \te{మాత్రమే}, \te{అయితే}, \te{తరువాత}, \te{ఇంకా} are what turn a set of separate answers into a conversation.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \te{కూడా}, \te{మాత్రమే}, \te{అయితే}, \te{తరువాత}, \te{ఇంకా}. Enough to add to an answer, limit it, order it, or keep it open.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{iṅkā}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then answer \emph{antē?} with \emph{iṅkā undi}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{ఇంకా} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}still, yet\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
